title: Peripheral Neuropathy
subject: Medicine
summary: Peripheral neuropathy is damage to peripheral nerves causing sensory, motor and autonomic deficits. In low‑resource settings tropical infections, HIV, TB treatment and diabetes are common causes. Diagnosis relies on focused history, bedside examination and targeted investigations.

sections.p: Peripheral neuropathy denotes dysfunction of peripheral nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, producing sensory loss, weakness, pain or autonomic change. Diagnosis requires a compatible clinical picture and exclusion of central causes.
b: Sensory: glove‑and‑stocking numbness, burning, tingling
Motor: distal weakness, foot drop
Autonomic: orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis

t.b: What is the likely aetiology? – Identifies risk factors (diabetes, HIV, TB drugs, malnutrition, herbal toxins).
Is the pattern length‑dependent? – Confirms peripheral distribution and helps stage severity.

sections.p: The Toronto Clinical Scoring System (TCSS) grades severity from 0 (none) to 19 (severe) using symptoms, reflexes and sensory testing; higher scores predict functional loss and ulcer risk.
b: TCSS 0‑5: mild
TCSS 6‑11: moderate
TCSS ≥12: severe

sections.p: In East African hospitals the hierarchy of causes is:
b: 1. Diabetes mellitus (type 2, long‑standing)
2. Isoniazid therapy for TB (often without pyridoxine)
3. HIV infection and antiretrovirals (stavudine, zidovudine)
4. Chronic kidney disease (uremia)
5. Nutritional deficiencies (vitamin B12, thiamine)
6. Tropical infections (leprosy, malaria, schistosomiasis)
7. Alcohol excess

sections.p: Patients usually report progressive distal numbness and burning that starts in the feet and ascends. Weakness may cause gait instability or foot drop. Autonomic symptoms are often overlooked but may include dry skin, constipation or orthostatic dizziness.
b: Symmetrical glove‑and‑stocking sensory loss
Reduced or absent ankle reflexes
Positive Romberg sign if proprioception lost
Foot ulcer risk when loss of protective sensation

sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; when a test is unavailable, use bedside alternatives.

t.b: Is diabetes the cause? – Elevated glucose/HbA1c confirms diabetic neuropathy.
Is a nutritional deficiency present? – Low B12 points to megaloblastic neuropathy.
Is HIV infection contributing? – Positive test prompts ART review.
Is uremic neuropathy likely? – Elevated creatinine supports CKD‑related neuropathy.
Is the neuropathy demyelinating or axonal? – Slowed conduction velocity suggests demyelination; low amplitude suggests axonal loss.

t.a: Skin biopsy for intra‑epidermal nerve fibre density (rarely available)
t.b: Confirm small‑fiber loss when symptoms out of proportion to large‑fiber signs.

sections.p: Certain features demand urgent evaluation because they signal rapid progression or systemic danger.
b: Rapidly ascending weakness (possible Guillain‑Barré)
Severe autonomic instability (orthostatic shock, cardiac arrhythmia)
Unexplained weight loss or fever (infection, malignancy)
New foot ulcer or gangrene

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide symptomatic and preventive care.
b: Diabetes: optimise glycaemic control; metformin or insulin as per protocol.
HIV‑related: switch stavudine to tenofovir‑based regimen if possible; continue ART.
CKD: dialysis optimisation, avoid neurotoxic drugs.
Nutritional: replace deficient vitamins (B12 injection, thiamine).
Pain: start duloxetine or gabapentin (avoid tramadol if hepatic disease).
Foot care: daily inspection, proper footwear, treat ulcers promptly.

sections.p: Regular review prevents progression and complications.
b: Quarterly TCSS assessment to track severity.
Annual foot examination for ulcer detection.
Education on glucose control, avoidance of alcohol, and safe footwear.
Vaccination against hepatitis B and tetanus in at‑risk patients.
Radiculopathy – nerve root pain radiates, often with dermatomal pattern and positive straight‑leg raise.
Peripheral vascular disease – claudication improves with rest, pulses reduced, not sensory loss.
Central spinal cord lesion – presents with level‑specific weakness, hyperreflexia, and sensory level.
Normal nerve conduction studies early in small‑fiber neuropathy – rely on clinical picture.
Normal fasting glucose with high HbA1c – post‑prandial spikes cause neuropathy.
Normal vitamin B12 level but functional deficiency (elevated MMA) – consider testing MMA if suspicion high.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive weakness or respiratory compromise
New foot ulcer with signs of infection

faq.a: It depletes pyridoxine, a co‑factor for neurotransmitter synthesis, leading to axonal injury.

faq.q: Can a patient have neuropathy with normal reflexes?
faq.a: Early small‑fiber neuropathy may spare reflexes; loss appears later.

faq.q: Is duloxetine safe in patients with hepatitis?
faq.a: It is metabolised hepatically; avoid if liver enzymes >3 × ULN.

exam: A 55‑year‑old diabetic presents with burning feet and a new foot ulcer – what investigations and management steps are essential? — Check HbA1c, foot exam, start pyridoxine if on TB meds, optimise glucose, start duloxetine, arrange podiatry.
How does the Toronto Clinical Scoring System guide prognosis? — Scores ≥12 predict ulceration and functional loss, prompting intensive foot care and physiotherapy.
A HIV‑positive man on stavudine reports tingling in his hands – what alternative ART would you consider and why? — Switch to tenofovir‑based regimen; stavudine is neurotoxic and lipodystrophic.

What bedside sign differentiates peripheral neuropathy from peripheral arterial disease? — Loss of protective sensation with normal pulses suggests neuropathy; diminished pulses suggest arterial disease.

A patient with CKD stage 5 has glove‑and‑stocking numbness – which lab result supports uremic neuropathy and what is the treatment focus? — Elevated creatinine >5 mg/dL; optimise dialysis and avoid neurotoxic drugs.
When is urgent referral indicated for a patient with peripheral neuropathy? — Rapidly ascending weakness, autonomic crisis, or infected foot ulcer requiring surgical input.
Why might nerve conduction studies be normal in a patient with severe pain? — Small‑fiber neuropathy can cause pain without large‑fiber involvement; NCS may be normal.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect a focused history and perform a systematic neurological exam, noting sensory, motor, and autonomic features. Bedside tests reveal functional deficits but cannot quantify axonal loss or differentiate demyelinating from axonal patterns.
b: History: onset, progression, pain quality, distribution, precipitating factors, medication list, alcohol use, diabetes control, TB treatment, ART regimen, nutritional status, pregnancy, renal function

t.b: Assesses S1/S2 root integrity; absent suggests peripheral neuropathy but cannot distinguish axonal vs demyelinating
Loss indicates large‑fiber involvement; normal vibration (>15 s) rules out severe large‑fiber loss but does not exclude small‑fiber disease

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use targeted investigations to confirm etiology, quantify severity, and guide therapy. When resources are limited, bedside surrogates are acceptable.
b: Serum B12 <200 pmol/L (or <270 pg/mL) with raised MMA/homocysteine confirms functional deficiency; normal B12 but high MMA suggests folate deficiency
HbA1c >7 % indicates poor glycaemic control; target <7 % for neuropathy prevention
Serum creatinine/eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² signals uremic neuropathy; monitor urea and electrolytes
Peripheral nerve conduction studies (PNCS): reduced amplitude = axonal loss; slowed conduction = demyelination; normal PNCS with pain suggests small‑fiber neuropathy
Quantitative sensory testing (QST) for small fibres; abnormal thresholds support small‑fiber involvement
Skin biopsy for intra‑epidermal nerve fibre density (IENFD) when available; <5 fibres/mm² indicates small‑fiber neuropathy
Serum protein electrophoresis: any monoclonal spike, even <10 g/L, warrants further workup for paraproteinemia
HbA1c and fasting glucose if diabetes suspected

t.b: Answers: Is the neuropathy axonal or demyelinating? Normal PNCS with pain suggests small‑fiber disease
Answers: Is small‑fiber dysfunction present? Abnormal thresholds indicate small‑fiber neuropathy
Answers: Quantify small‑fiber loss; IENFD <5 fibres/mm² confirms small‑fiber neuropathy
Answers: Is B12 deficiency present? <200 pmol/L with raised MMA confirms deficiency
Answers: Is lead exposure likely? >5 µg/dL warrants chelation

sections.p: Diagnosis follows a stepwise approach: clinical features, laboratory confirmation, and electrophysiology. Severity is graded by the Toronto Clinical Scoring System (TCSS).
b: Clinical diagnosis: Symmetric glove‑and‑stocking sensory loss, distal weakness, absent ankle reflexes, and autonomic signs; exclude vascular causes
Laboratory confirmation: B12, folate, HIV, renal function, lead, electrolytes
Electrophysiology: PNCS or QST to classify axonal vs demyelinating vs small‑fiber
TCSS grading: 0–5 mild, 6–11 moderate, ≥12 severe; score derived from symptoms, reflexes, and sensory tests

t.b: Answers: Severity of neuropathy; guides prognosis and need for referral

sections.p: Several disorders mimic peripheral neuropathy; distinguishing features are highlighted.

t.b: Sudden focal weakness, cranial nerve involvement, and altered consciousness; neuroimaging confirms.
Relapsing–remitting course, optic neuritis, and MRI lesions; sensory loss is patchy, not glove‑and‑stocking.
Bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and bruising; sensory loss is uncommon.
Anxiety, abdominal pain, and wrist drop; blood lead >5 µg/dL confirms.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides treatment from reversible causes to symptomatic control, with clear points for monitoring and referral.
b: 2. Provide disease‑modifying measures where evidence exists – tight blood pressure control in CKD, treat B12 deficiency with intramuscular cyanocobalamin.
3. Initiate first‑line symptomatic therapy – duloxetine, amitriptyline, or gabapentin/pregabalin, choosing based on comorbidities and renal function.
4. Add adjunctive measures – foot care education, protective footwear, smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, physiotherapy for strength and balance.
5. Monitor response every 3 months with TCSS or pain VAS; document ulcer healing, reflex changes, and medication side‑effects.
6. Escalate to second‑line agents (e.g., tramadol, capsaicin patches) if pain remains moderate‑severe after 8 weeks of first‑line therapy.
7. Refer urgently for rapid progression, motor weakness, autonomic crisis, or suspected Guillain‑Barré; also refer to neurology for abnormal NCS/EMG or when diagnosis remains unclear.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, drug‑drug interactions and practical steps to mitigate them.
b: Duloxetine – may raise blood pressure and cause nausea; check BP each visit, avoid in uncontrolled hypertension.
Amitriptyline – anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention) and cardiac conduction delay; obtain baseline ECG in patients >60 y or with cardiac disease.
Gabapentin/pregabalin – dizziness, peripheral oedema; start low, counsel on fall risk, adjust dose if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
Tricyclics + MAO inhibitors – risk of serotonin syndrome; review medication list for antidepressants, linezolid, tramadol.
NSAIDs – worsen renal function and ulcer risk; avoid in CKD stage 4‑5, use gastro‑protection if needed.
Opioids (e.g., tramadol) – respiratory depression, dependence; reserve for refractory pain, limit duration, monitor for constipation.

sections.p: Complications arise from loss of sensation, autonomic dysfunction or disease progression; early recognition triggers referral.
b: Foot ulcer or Charcot joint – inspect feet daily; if ulcer >2 cm, deep, or infected, refer to wound‑care team and consider off‑loading.
Falls and fractures – assess gait, Romberg, and ankle reflex; arrange physiotherapy and orthotics if balance impaired.
Autonomic crisis (orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis) – measure supine and standing BP; treat with fluid, compression stockings, and consider fludrocortisone.
Rapidly ascending weakness or bulbar signs – suspect Guillain‑Barré; arrange urgent neurology referral and consider IVIG/plasma exchange.
Severe pain unresponsive to two first‑line agents after 8 weeks – add second‑line analgesic and refer for specialist pain management.

sections.p: Conditions that modify presentation, investigations or therapy.
b: HIV – may cause distal sensory polyneuropathy; viral load and CD4 guide ART change; avoid stavudine and zidovudine.
TB treatment – isoniazid depletes pyridoxine; give prophylactic pyridoxine to all patients on INH, especially malnourished.
Malnutrition – B12, thiamine, folate deficiencies mimic neuropathy; check serum B12 (<200 pmol/L) and MMA, treat with appropriate vitamins.
Alcohol excess – contributes to axonal loss; counsel cessation, assess liver function before prescribing hepatotoxic agents.
Renal failure – gabapentin/pregabalin require dose reduction; avoid NSAIDs; dialysis patients may have uremic neuropathy, treat with dialysis optimisation.
Liver disease – limit duloxetine and amitriptyline; monitor transaminases if using tricyclics.
Age extremes – children have different normal reflex patterns; elderly have higher fall risk and altered drug clearance.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for vulnerable populations and low‑resource environments.
b: Children – neuropathy rare; focus on chemotherapy‑induced or hereditary causes; use age‑appropriate pain scales, avoid tricyclics due to cardiac risk.
Pregnancy – prioritize non‑pharmacologic measures; if medication required, use low‑dose amitriptyline or duloxetine after risk‑benefit discussion.
Elderly – start all drugs at lowest effective dose; prefer gabapentin/pregabalin with renal adjustment; monitor cognition and fall risk.
People with HIV – switch from stavudine to tenofovir‑based regimen; screen for opportunistic infections that can cause neuropathy.
Low‑resource settings – use bedside tests (monofilament, tuning fork >15 s) when NCS unavailable; pyridoxine supplementation is cheap and essential with INH; prioritize foot care education.

facts: Toronto Clinical Scoring System (TCSS) 0‑5 mild, 6‑11 moderate, ≥12 severe.
Serum vitamin B12 <200 pmol/L (or <270 pg/mL) defines deficiency.
Blood lead level >5 µg/dL (0.24 µmol/L) is elevated.
Vibration sense with 128‑Hz tuning fork normal >15 seconds, abnormal <1 second.
Ankle reflex (S1‑S2) mediated primarily by the S1 spinal nerve root.
Isoniazid causes pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency → axonal degeneration.
First‑line symptomatic agents for painful neuropathy: duloxetine, amitriptyline, gabapentin/pregabalin.
Stavudine, zidovudine and other d4T‑based regimens cause distal sensory neuropathy.
Uremic neuropathy associated with serum creatinine >500 µmol/L (stage 5 CKD).
Alcohol‑related neuropathy linked to >80 g/day ethanol for >5 years.

vivas.q: Define peripheral neuropathy and its three clinical domains.
vivas.a: Dysfunction of peripheral nerves causing sensory (glove‑and‑stocking numbness, burning), motor (distal weakness, foot drop) and autonomic (orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis) deficits.

vivas.q: What is the Toronto Clinical Scoring System and how does it guide prognosis?
vivas.a: TCSS scores symptoms, reflexes and sensory testing (0‑19). Scores ≥12 predict severe disability and higher ulcer risk; ≤5 predicts mild disease with good recovery.

vivas.q: A diabetic patient presents with burning feet and a new ulcer. What investigations do you order first?
vivas.a: Fasting glucose/HbA1c, serum B12, renal function, nerve conduction study if available, foot X‑ray to assess osteomyelitis, and wound swab for culture.

vivas.q: Why is duloxetine considered symptomatic, not disease‑modifying, for diabetic neuropathy?
vivas.a: It modulates central serotonin/norepinephrine pathways to reduce pain perception but does not halt nerve degeneration.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate peripheral neuropathy from peripheral arterial disease at the bedside?
vivas.a: Peripheral neuropathy shows sensory loss with preserved pulses; PAD shows diminished pulses, cool skin, and pain on exertion relieved by rest.

vivas.q: Interpret a serum B12 of 110 pmol/L with normal folate in a vegan patient.
vivas.a: Deficiency confirmed; start high‑dose oral or IM B12 and assess MMA/homocysteine if available.

vivas.q: When is urgent referral indicated for peripheral neuropathy?
vivas.a: Rapidly ascending weakness, autonomic crisis, severe pain unresponsive to analgesia, or suspicion of Guillain‑Barré, vasculitic or infectious cause.

vivas.q: A patient on high‑dose isoniazid develops neuropathy. Which vitamin must be supplemented and why?
vivas.a: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) prevents axonal degeneration caused by isoniazid‑induced B6 depletion.

vivas.q: Explain the mechanism of vincristine‑induced neuropathy.
vivas.a: Vincristine binds tubulin, inhibiting microtubule polymerisation, which disrupts axonal transport leading to axonal degeneration.

vivas.q: Which spinal nerve root level mediates the ankle reflex?
What is the key history to ask a patient with suspected toxic neuropathy?
vivas.a: Duration and dose of offending drug, alcohol intake, nutritional status, HIV/TB status, and recent infections.

vivas.q: How does HIV‑related neuropathy differ from diabetic neuropathy?
vivas.a: Often painful, distal, may involve small fibers early; associated with low CD4 count and stavudine exposure.

vivas.q: Why might nerve conduction studies be normal in a patient with severe neuropathic pain?
vivas.a: Small‑fiber neuropathy affects pain fibers that are not assessed by standard NCS, giving normal results despite severe symptoms.

vivas.q: What are red‑flag features that suggest a non‑diabetic cause of neuropathy?
vivas.a: Rapid progression, asymmetric distribution, prominent autonomic failure, associated systemic illness (e.g., HIV, TB, CKD), or exposure to neurotoxic drugs.

vivas.q: What is the recommended approach when a bedside test (e.g., monofilament) is unavailable?
vivas.a: Use 10‑g Semmes‑Weinstein monofilament substitute (paper clip) or assess protective sensation by pinprick and vibration.

mcqs.q: A 58‑year‑old man with long‑standing type 2 diabetes presents with symmetric stocking‑glove numbness, absent ankle reflexes and a 0‑second vibration sense at the great toe. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
mcqs.e: Amitriptyline is first‑line symptomatic therapy for painful diabetic neuropathy.

mcqs.q: Which antiretroviral drug is most strongly associated with distal sensory neuropathy?
mcqs.e: Stavudine (d4T) causes mitochondrial toxicity leading to neuropathy.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old with CKD stage 5 complains of glove‑and‑stocking numbness. Which finding supports uremic neuropathy?
mcqs.e: Uremic neuropathy appears in advanced renal failure, typically creatinine >500 µmol/L.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a microtubule‑disrupting plant‑derived chemotherapy agent that commonly causes severe peripheral neuropathy and paralytic ileus?
mcqs.e: Vincristine binds tubulin, disrupting microtubules and causing neuropathy and ileus.

mcqs.q: A vegan patient presents with megaloblastic anemia and peripheral neuropathy. Which metabolic block explains the neuropathy?
mcqs.e: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs methylmalonyl‑CoA mutase, leading to accumulation of toxic metabolites affecting nerves.

mcqs.q: A patient on high‑dose isoniazid develops neuropathy. Which drug should be given prophylactically to prevent this complication?
mcqs.e: Pyridoxine supplementation prevents isoniazid‑induced B6 deficiency and neuropathy.

cases.v: 45‑year‑old male, type 2 diabetic for 12 years, presents with burning feet for 6 months, new plantar ulcer, absent ankle reflexes, vibration <1 s at great toe.

qs.q: What is the most likely primary diagnosis?
qs.a: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy with a neuro‑ulcer.
HbA1c, serum B12, renal function, foot X‑ray, wound culture, and if possible nerve conduction study.
Optimize glycaemic control, start amitriptyline for pain, debride ulcer, off‑load foot, start appropriate antibiotics if infection, and arrange podiatry follow‑up.

cases.v: 30‑year‑old woman, newly diagnosed HIV, on stavudine‑based ART, complains of tingling in both hands and feet, normal ankle reflexes, vibration 2 s, CD4 180 cells/µL.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of her neuropathy?
What modification to her regimen should be considered?
qs.a: Switch to a non‑neurotoxic regimen (e.g., tenofovir + lamivudine + efavirenz) and add symptomatic therapy if pain persists.

qs.q: Which bedside test can help confirm large‑fiber involvement?
qs.a: 128‑Hz tuning fork vibration; <1 s indicates large‑fiber loss.

mistakes: Confusing the normal vibration cut‑off (>15 s) with <8 s; use >15 s as normal.
Using serum B12 <150 pmol/L as deficiency; correct threshold is <200 pmol/L.
Stating duloxetine is contraindicated in renal impairment; it requires dose adjustment only when eGFR <30 mL/min.
Describing gabapentin as only for mixed neuropathic pain; it is first‑line for painful diabetic neuropathy.
Claiming high‑dose diuretics worsen gabapentin‑induced edema; diuretics may actually manage the edema.
Suggesting tramadol as first‑line for neuropathic pain; it is not recommended as first‑line in low‑resource settings.
Attributing isoniazid neuropathy primarily to impaired myelin synthesis; the main mechanism is axonal degeneration due to B6 deficiency.
Assuming a monofilament test can differentiate arterial from neuropathic disease; pulse examination is required.
